# Introduction

## Problem Statement

### The Problem:

Autonomous-vehicle pick-up / drop-off (PUDO) maneuvers — the moments a driverless
vehicle stops so a rider can get in or out — are a plausible source of curb-space
conflict, minor collisions, and rider complaints. Whether that risk is growing,
shrinking, or holding steady as a fleet scales is hard to answer from the public
record: California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) AV Deployment reports are
large, redacted, and change format from quarter to quarter, so nobody has simply
lined them up into a rate over time.

### Contribution

- A reproducible pipeline (`pudo-pipeline`) that ingests nine CPUC quarterly
  report zips for Waymo's driverless deployment — two incompatible file schemas,
  redaction, and formatting drift included — into five analysis-ready tables.
- An exposure-adjusted PUDO complaint rate across eight quarters
  (2024 Q3 – 2026 Q2), on trips — the team's chosen exposure measure, cross-checked
  against total vehicle miles traveled — with an explicit primary trend test
  (Negative-Binomial GLM, after Poisson regression was diagnosed as
  overdispersed), a launch-period sensitivity analysis isolating the 2024
  deployment ramp, a distribution-free cross-check (Mann-Kendall), and a
  Bayesian refit (PyMC/NUTS) that reports a direct posterior probability the
  rate is declining alongside the frequentist p-value.
- A placement of the PUDO hazard on a probability × impact risk matrix that is
  computed from the data rather than asserted, with the probability basis left
  as a visible, toggleable assumption.

### Scope and Vision

**Scope:** one carrier (Waymo), one state (California), eight quarters, public
CPUC filings only — no proprietary telemetry. **Vision:** the pipeline's loaders
are written against the CPUC's public template, not against Waymo specifically,
so the same numerator/denominator/trend method can be pointed at any other
CPUC-reporting AV carrier to support carrier-to-carrier comparison rather than a
single-carrier trend.

## Technical Challenges

- **Two incompatible numerator schemas.** 2024 reports ship one aggregate,
  pre-summed row per quarter; 2025Q1 onward ship ride-level microdata (millions
  of rows) with a Y/N complaint flag. Both had to be reconciled into one
  numerator, and the level shift between eras cannot be fully ruled out.
- **Redaction.** Incident timestamps, locations, and the `PUDOTravelLane` flag
  are blank in every file of every period, ruling out within-quarter timing or
  spatial analysis.
- **Silent formatting drift.** Comma-grouped numerics, filenames that change
  across quarters, and a transposed carrier ID silently nulled the exposure
  data until caught — the loader now warns loudly instead of nulling quietly.
- **Non-calendar reporting periods.** The 2024 CPUC reports are not calendar
  quarters, so "2024 Q3" / "2024 Q4" needed explicit relabeling (`period_label`,
  `is_calendar_quarter`) to avoid silently comparing the wrong months.
- **Small, overdispersed counts.** 27–79 complaints per quarter is enough to
  rule out the normal-approximation trend test, but not enough to ignore
  quarter-to-quarter noise.

# Data

## Data Sources

Public data comes from the CPUC AV Program's quarterly deployment reports
(cpuc.ca.gov → Licensing → Autonomous Vehicle Programs → Quarterly Reporting) [@cpuc_av_quarterly_reporting].
Two file families, both filed per reporting period:

- **Incidents-Complaints** — the numerator. PUDO complaint and PUDO-collision
  counts.
- **Month-Level** — the denominator. Real `Year`/`Month`, trips, and vehicle
  miles traveled (VMT). VMT is further split into three "period" columns in
  the source file, but CPUC's own reference key never defines what those
  periods mean, so this analysis uses trips as the primary exposure measure
  and VMT only as an unsplit, whole-quarter cross-check.

Nine raw reporting windows (Jun–Aug 2024, Sep–Nov 2024, a Dec 2024 one-month
stub, then eight calendar quarters through 2026 Q2) are recombined into eight
analysis quarters, `2024Q3`–`2026Q2`.

The pipeline's two upstream file families reduce to a single hand-off table,
`final_pudo_summary` — one row per analysis quarter, carrying only the
complaint numerator and the trips denominator (@tbl-final-data). This is the
dataset the rest of the paper's analysis runs on:

{{< include assets/tbl-final-data.md >}}

All numbers, tables, and figures in this paper are pulled directly from the
project's analysis notebook — see
[`pudo_analysis.ipynb`](https://github.com/jonathanwilsonami/curbrisk-av/blob/main/pudo-pipeline/notebooks/pudo_analysis.ipynb)
for the full code and every intermediate result.

# Methods

## Feature Engineering

Every analysis period carries a clean sort/filter key (`period_id`) alongside a
human-readable label, its exact date window, and a flag for whether that window
is actually a calendar quarter (`period_label`, `window_start`/`window_end`,
`is_calendar_quarter` — false only for the two 2024 periods). Two exposure
denominators are computed per period — trips (one pick-up + one drop-off per
trip, the most literal PUDO-opportunity count; the primary measure) and total
VMT (a cross-check) — each paired with a `pudo_per_100k_*` rate, plus a
PUDO-share-of-all-complaints column for context.

## Modeling

PUDO complaints were initially modeled using Poisson regression with the
logarithm of trip exposure included as an offset. A variance-to-mean
dispersion diagnostic (@eq-dispersion) showed substantial overdispersion in
the quarterly counts ($\text{VMR} \approx 5.9$), violating the Poisson
equidispersion assumption. Temporal trends were therefore estimated using
**Negative-Binomial regression** with a log link and a trip-exposure offset as
the primary model. Because only eight quarterly observations were available,
the same model was additionally estimated in a **Bayesian framework** to more
fully characterize parameter and dispersion uncertainty. The Poisson fit below
is retained only as an initial diagnostic baseline — it is never reported as
the trend result.

### Poisson regression (initial diagnostic baseline)

The complaint count $Y_t$ in analysis quarter $t = 0, \dots, 7$ is first
modeled as a Poisson process whose rate scales with exposure $E_t$ (trips, or
VMT as a cross-check), with a log-linear time trend:

$$
Y_t \mid \mu_t \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_t), \qquad
\log \mu_t = \log E_t + \beta_0 + \beta_1 t
$$ {#eq-poisson-glm}

$\log E_t$ enters with a fixed coefficient of 1 (an *offset*), so $\beta_1$ is
the log change in the underlying **rate** $\mu_t / E_t$ per quarter, not in the
raw count. Every incidence rate ratio (IRR) and "per-quarter % change" quoted
in this paper, for whichever model produced $\beta_1$, is:

$$
\text{IRR} = e^{\beta_1}, \qquad
\text{\% change per quarter} = \big(e^{\beta_1} - 1\big) \times 100\%
$$ {#eq-pct-change}

### Overdispersion check

@eq-poisson-glm's defining assumption is $\text{Var}(Y_t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_t]$.
This is checked with the index of dispersion (variance-to-mean ratio, VMR) on
the raw complaint counts across the $n = 8$ quarters:

$$
\text{VMR} = \frac{s^2}{\bar{y}}, \qquad
D = (n-1)\,\text{VMR} \;\sim\; \chi^2_{n-1} \ \text{ under } H_0 : \text{Poisson}
$$ {#eq-dispersion}

$\text{VMR} \approx 1$ is consistent with a pure Poisson process; $\text{VMR}
\gg 1$ — the result found here (VMR ≈ 5.9) — rejects equidispersion, so the
Poisson fit's confidence interval and $p$-value understate uncertainty and are
not used for inference about the trend.

### Negative-Binomial regression (primary trend model)

Because @eq-dispersion rejects equidispersion, the trend is instead estimated
with Negative-Binomial regression (the NB2 parametrization used by
`statsmodels`), keeping the same log-linear mean structure and offset as
@eq-poisson-glm:

$$
Y_t \mid \mu_t, \alpha \sim \text{NB}(\mu_t, \alpha), \qquad
\text{Var}(Y_t) = \mu_t + \alpha\,\mu_t^2, \qquad
\log \mu_t = \log E_t + \beta_0 + \beta_1 t
$$ {#eq-nb2}

with the dispersion parameter $\alpha$ estimated by maximum likelihood
alongside $\beta_0, \beta_1$ (larger $\alpha$ means *more* overdispersion
relative to Poisson under this parametrization). This is the paper's
**primary frequentist trend model**, reported with $\beta_1$, its standard
error, 95% confidence interval, $p$-value, and the incidence rate ratio and
percent change of @eq-pct-change.

### Launch-period sensitivity

2024 Q3–Q4 read as a deployment/launch ramp, with substantially higher
exposure-adjusted rates than 2025 onward (@fig-trend-fit). Rather than simply
discarding those quarters, @eq-nb2 is re-estimated — same model form, same
trip-exposure offset — on two pre-registered windows to test whether they
drive the full-period result:

- **A. Full period** — 2024 Q3 – 2026 Q2 ($n = 8$; the primary model above)
- **B. Post-ramp** — 2025 Q1 – 2026 Q2 ($n = 6$; excludes both 2024 quarters)

Comparing $\beta_1$, its confidence interval, and its $p$-value across the two
windows indicates whether the apparent decline is concentrated in the launch
period or continues afterward. Given $n = 8$, a simple two-window comparison
is used rather than a piecewise or launch-indicator model, to avoid
introducing more parameters than the data can support.

### Exact (Garwood) Poisson confidence interval

Uncertainty around each **observed** quarter's count is reported with the
exact Poisson interval rather than the normal/Wald approximation, so it stays
valid at small or zero counts:

$$
\text{CI}_{1-\alpha}(k) = \left[\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^2_{\alpha/2}(2k),\;\;
\tfrac{1}{2}\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2}(2k+2)\right] \Big/ E \;\times\; 10^5
$$ {#eq-exact-ci}

where $\chi^2_{p}(\nu)$ is the $p$-quantile of a chi-square distribution with
$\nu$ degrees of freedom, $k$ the observed complaint count, and $E$ the
exposure (trips) for that quarter. This interval is **descriptive**: it
summarizes uncertainty around one observed quarter's count/rate. It is
distinct from — and not a substitute for — @eq-nb2's *inferential* uncertainty
about the trend across quarters; overlapping exact Poisson intervals between
quarters do not, by themselves, establish that no trend exists.

### Distribution-free trend check (robustness)

As a **robustness check** that assumes no particular count distribution — not
a replacement for the primary Negative-Binomial fit — Kendall's $\tau$ is
computed between the quarter index and the per-quarter rate $r_1, \dots, r_n$
(chronological order):

$$
\tau = \frac{2}{n(n-1)} \sum_{i < j} \text{sign}\big(r_j - r_i\big)
$$ {#eq-kendall}

$\tau < 0$ agrees with a declining trend; its $p$-value is reported alongside,
separately from the NB model's.

### Bayesian Negative-Binomial refit

Because only eight quarterly observations are available, @eq-nb2 is
additionally estimated in a Bayesian framework to more fully characterize
parameter *and* dispersion uncertainty — the frequentist fit instead estimates
$\alpha$ by maximum likelihood and then treats it as *known*, relying on a
large-sample approximation that a sample this small may not support. The same
likelihood and exposure structure as @eq-nb2 is refit as a full posterior
(PyMC, NUTS sampler) with weakly informative priors:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_0 &\sim \mathcal{N}\!\big(\log(\bar{r}),\, 2^2\big) \\
\beta_1 &\sim \mathcal{N}(0,\, 1^2) \\
\alpha &\sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
\mu_t &= E_t \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 t) \\
Y_t \mid \mu_t, \alpha &\sim \text{NB}(\mu_t, \alpha), \qquad
\text{Var}(Y_t) = \mu_t + \mu_t^2/\alpha
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-bayes-nb}

where $\bar{r}$ is the pooled baseline rate and $\beta_1 \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$
deliberately expresses no prior belief about direction. Note @eq-bayes-nb's
variance term is the **inverse** sense of @eq-nb2's $\alpha$ (larger $\alpha$
here means *closer* to Poisson) — the two are not numerically comparable. The
model is sampled with 4 chains × 2000 draws, checked for convergence
($\hat{R}$, effective sample size, divergence count) and for sensitivity to
the prior width on $\beta_1$. The quantity of interest is the posterior
probability the rate is actually declining, estimated directly from the
fraction of posterior draws below zero rather than from a $p$-value:

$$
P(\text{declining}) = P(\beta_1 < 0 \mid y_{1:n})
$$ {#eq-p-declining}

This Bayesian refit is reported as a robustness / small-sample analysis
alongside the frequentist estimate, not as a claim that it fits the data
better: no model-comparison criterion (e.g. WAIC/LOO) or posterior-predictive
check is computed here, so no such claim is made.

### Risk-matrix probability basis

To place the PUDO hazard on a probability × impact risk matrix, three ways of
expressing "how likely is a PUDO event" are compared, holding the impact
reading fixed. Let $k = \sum_t y_t$ be total complaints and
$N = \sum_t E_t$ total trips over the window.

**Per-period** — the probability of at least one complaint in a reporting
quarter, treating the mean quarterly count $\bar\lambda = k/n$ as a Poisson
rate:

$$
p_{\text{per-period}} = 1 - e^{-\bar\lambda}
$$ {#eq-prob-period}

**Per-trip** — the raw empirical per-trip probability:

$$
p_{\text{per-trip}} = \frac{k}{N}
$$ {#eq-prob-trip}

**Bayesian** — a Beta-Binomial posterior on the per-trip rate (Jeffreys-style
$\text{Beta}(0.5, 0.5)$ prior), converted to a predictive probability of at
least one complaint in a future quarter of size $E_{\text{next}}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{rate} \mid k, N &\sim \text{Beta}(0.5 + k,\ 0.5 + N - k) \\
p_{\text{bayesian}} &= 1 - e^{-\widehat{\text{rate}}\; \cdot\; E_{\text{next}}}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-prob-bayes}

using the posterior mean $\widehat{\text{rate}}$ and the most recent quarter's
trip volume as $E_{\text{next}}$.

# Evaluation and Results

Per-quarter descriptive statistics for the complaint counts, exposure, and rate
(@tbl-summary-stats) show why raw counts cannot be compared directly: exposure
grows nearly 6× across the window.

{{< include assets/tbl-summary-stats.md >}}

The index-of-dispersion test (@eq-dispersion) on these counts gives
$\text{VMR} \approx 5$ ($D \approx 41.5$ against $\chi^2_7$, $p < 0.001$),
rejecting Poisson equidispersion — the reason every trend fit below uses the
Negative-Binomial model of @eq-nb2 rather than @eq-poisson-glm directly. The
per-quarter rates in @tbl-baseline and throughout use the exact interval of
@eq-exact-ci, not a normal approximation.

Pooling across all eight quarters gives the headline exposure-adjusted rate
(@tbl-baseline):
{{< include assets/baseline-headline.md >}}

{{< include assets/tbl-baseline.md >}}

PUDO complaints are also worth reading in context of everything else riders
report. @fig-pudo-share stacks the PUDO count against every other reported
complaint category, per quarter:

![PUDO complaints against all other reported complaint categories, per
quarter.](assets/fig-pudo-share.png){#fig-pudo-share}

{{< include assets/pudo-share-headline.md >}}
PUDO complaints scale with total complaint volume — the PUDO share stays in a
fairly narrow band rather than drifting — so PUDO is not a shrinking or
growing slice of the overall complaint mix; it is consistently the largest
category tied to a specific vehicle maneuver rather than a general safety or
"other" catch-all.

### Primary trend: Negative-Binomial regression

The primary trend model — @eq-nb2 fit on trips exposure — gives (@tbl-nb-primary):
{{< include assets/trend-primary-headline.md >}}

{{< include assets/tbl-nb-primary.md >}}

In plain language: each additional quarter multiplies the expected PUDO
complaint rate per trip by the incidence rate ratio (IRR) in @tbl-nb-primary,
holding exposure fixed. The Poisson diagnostic fit (@eq-poisson-glm) is not
reported here as an inferential result — it assumes equidispersion, which
@eq-dispersion rejects.

![Observed PUDO complaint rate per 100k trips (exact Poisson 95% CI, a
descriptive interval around each observed quarter) against the Negative-
Binomial fitted trend and its own 95% model-based confidence
band.](assets/fig-trend-fit.png){#fig-trend-fit}

@fig-trend-fit keeps the two kinds of uncertainty visually distinct: the blue
error bars are @eq-exact-ci, describing each observed quarter's count; the
red band is the NB regression's uncertainty about the *trend line* itself.
The two 2024 quarters sit well above the rest of the series and above the
fitted line's lower band — a sharp drop from a launch-period high, followed by
a rate that moves within a fairly narrow range for the remaining six quarters.
The overlapping bars from 2025 onward describe individual quarters and are not
by themselves evidence for or against a trend; that question is addressed
directly below.

### Launch-period sensitivity

Restricting the identical NB model to the post-ramp window tests whether the
full-period decline is concentrated in the 2024 launch quarters
(@tbl-launch-sensitivity):
{{< include assets/launch-sensitivity-headline.md >}}

{{< include assets/tbl-launch-sensitivity.md >}}

The post-ramp slope is close to zero and not statistically significant on its
own, in contrast to the full-period estimate. The apparent decline over the
full study period appears to be driven substantially by the elevated rates
observed during the 2024 launch period, while rates from 2025 onward appear
comparatively stable — consistent with a launch/ramp-period effect rather than
a continuing decline, though this does not establish causation.

### Robustness checks

Refitting @eq-nb2 under the VMT-total cross-check gives the same direction as
the primary trips-based fit, and Kendall's $\tau$ (@eq-kendall) — a
distribution-free check, not an alternative primary model — agrees in sign
under both denominators (@tbl-trend):
{{< include assets/trend-headline.md >}}

{{< include assets/tbl-trend.md >}}

Mann-Kendall's weaker significance reflects the non-monotone, fell-then-flat
shape of the series (limited power for a monotone-rank test on $n = 8$), not
evidence that the trend is absent.

### Bayesian robustness check

The Bayesian refit (@eq-bayes-nb, @tbl-bayes-nb) is reported alongside the
primary frequentist estimate as a small-sample robustness check — not a claim
that it fits the data better — and reports @eq-p-declining directly rather
than a $p$-value:
{{< include assets/bayes-trend-headline.md >}}

{{< include assets/tbl-bayes-nb.md >}}

![Bayesian Negative-Binomial posterior on the per-quarter rate change, vs. the
frequentist point estimate and 95% CI.](assets/fig-bayes-trend.png){#fig-bayes-trend}

The posterior barely shifts across a 4× range of prior width on the slope
(@tbl-bayes-prior-sensitivity) — the conclusion is driven by the data, not the
choice of prior:

{{< include assets/tbl-bayes-prior-sensitivity.md >}}

To place the hazard on a risk matrix, the consequence of a PUDO event is read
off a risk curve — how the event rate falls as severity rises (@fig-risk-curve).
Nothing severe or fatal was observed at the PUDO level over the window.

![PUDO risk curve: event rate per 100,000 trips at each step up in consequence
severity (log scale). The unfilled bar is a rule-of-three upper bound on a
rate with zero observed events, not a measurement.](assets/fig-risk-curve.png){#fig-risk-curve}

Combining that impact reading with a probability of a PUDO complaint occurring
in a given reporting quarter — @tbl-risk-basis compares the three formulas of
@eq-prob-period, @eq-prob-trip, and @eq-prob-bayes — places the hazard on the
matrix as follows:

# Discussion

## Key Concepts and Definitions

- **PUDO** — pick-up / drop-off: the maneuver where a vehicle stops to let a
  rider board or alight.
- **Exposure denominator** — the activity measure a complaint count is divided
  by (trips or VMT) so rates are comparable across quarters of very different
  fleet size.
- **Overdispersion** — when a count's variance exceeds its mean beyond what a
  Poisson process allows, indicating real between-period rate variation.
- **Risk matrix axes** — *Probability*: how likely the hazard is to occur in a
  given period; *Impact*: how severe the outcome is when it does.
- **Credible interval vs. confidence interval** — the Bayesian model's 95%
  credible interval is a direct probability statement ("there is a 95% chance
  the true slope is in this range, given the data and the prior"); the
  frequentist confidence interval is not, which is why the two are reported
  side by side rather than treated as interchangeable.
- **Descriptive vs. inferential interval** — the exact Poisson interval on
  each observed quarter (@eq-exact-ci) describes uncertainty around that
  quarter's *count*; the Negative-Binomial regression's confidence interval on
  $\beta_1$ describes uncertainty about the *trend across* quarters. They
  answer different questions, so overlapping per-quarter intervals are not
  evidence that no trend exists.

## Assumptions

- PUDO complaints are initially treated as a Poisson-type count process; the
  overdispersion test shows this assumption fails, so Negative-Binomial
  regression — not Poisson — is used for all trend inference.
- The Bayesian trend model's priors are weakly informative and were checked
  for sensitivity (@tbl-bayes-prior-sensitivity) — the posterior does not
  depend meaningfully on the specific prior width chosen.
- The risk matrix's "Almost certain" probability reading assumes the relevant
  question is *will at least one PUDO complaint occur somewhere in the fleet
  this quarter* (it will), not the odds for any single trip.
- Complaint counts are assumed complete and consistently defined within each
  reporting era; the 2024 aggregate table and the 2025+ ride-level microdata
  are assumed to measure the same underlying thing.

## Limitations

- Complaints are self-reported by the carrier to its regulator; the rate
  measures *reported* problems, not necessarily underlying PUDO behavior, and
  reporting propensity could itself change over time.
- Waymo expanded to new cities during the window; a rate change may partly
  reflect new-market composition rather than a change in PUDO behavior.
- The 2024 and 2025+ numerators come from different source-file schemas, so a
  level shift at that boundary cannot be fully distinguished from a real trend.
- The launch-period sensitivity check further shrinks an already-small sample
  (post-ramp $n = 6$), which limits its power: a non-significant post-ramp
  slope is also consistent with a real but smaller decline continuing, not
  only with no decline at all.
- Redaction removes all within-quarter timing and location detail, and the
  travel-lane PUDO signal is unavailable in every file.
- Single carrier, single state, eight quarters — not yet a cross-carrier or
  multi-state comparison.

# Conclusion and Future Work

Over 2024 Q3 – 2026 Q2, the primary Negative-Binomial trend model finds
Waymo's exposure-adjusted PUDO complaint rate falling by 10.7% per quarter
(95% CI −17.8% to −3.1%, $p = 0.007$) — not the rising trend a naive raw-count
reading would suggest. The launch-period sensitivity analysis indicates that
decline is driven substantially by the 2024 launch-ramp quarters: restricted
to 2025 Q1 – 2026 Q2, the slope is small and not statistically significant.
The Bayesian refit agrees in direction but is more cautious, putting the
posterior probability of an actual decline at about 90% rather than treating
the frequentist $p$-value as certainty. On a probability × impact risk matrix
the hazard currently sits in the **Medium**, monitor-and-mitigate band:
frequent enough to expect every quarter, but low-consequence, with no severe
or fatal PUDO events observed. These results are still provisional (see
Limitations) — in particular, the post-ramp window's small sample cannot rule
out a smaller ongoing decline, only a large one; as more CPUC quarters are
published the same pipeline can extend the trend directly, and applying it to
other CPUC-reporting AV carriers would turn a single-carrier trend into a
cross-carrier comparison.
